For positive integers $n$ and $p$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and define its (uncentered, unit-variance-normalized) sample covariance matrix by
$$S(X):=\frac1nX^{\mathsf T}X\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}.$$
It is real symmetric and non-negative. If its eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$, its empirical spectral distribution (ESD), normalized by the matrix dimension $p$, is
$$\mu_{S(X)}:=\frac1p\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}.$$
The largest eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\max}(S(X)):=\max_j\lambda_j(S(X))$. When $S(X)$ has at least one positive eigenvalue, its smallest positive eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S(X)):=\min\{\lambda_j(S(X)):\lambda_j(S(X))>0\}$. For a sequence $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$, write $S_n=S(X_n)$ and $\mu_n=\mu_{S_n}$.

existing_contract_evidence.quote: Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. For each $n$, let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,1\le j\le p_n}$ and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)$ denote its smallest positive eigenvalue whenever one exists. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full column rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has no zero eigenvalues eventually and $\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\to(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. If $\gamma>1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full row rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues and $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2$. If $\gamma=1$, then almost surely $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)\to0$.

existing_contract_evidence.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.
